summary.text: For an input of the form \(2^r+1\), all \(r\) residue terms equal \(1\), while for \(2^r+3\) the first residue is \(1\) and the remaining \(r-1\) residues are \(3\). Thus both \(2^{67}+1\) and \(2^{23}+3\) give the value \(67\), so there are at least two occurrences rather than one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k),
\]
so that \(F\) is sequence A049802. Thus \(a(n)\), sequence A383327, is the number of natural numbers \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\). We disprove the claimed statement by showing that \(67\), which is one of the listed values of \(n\), occurs at least twice in A049802.

We will use the elementary fact that if \(k\le r\), then \(2^k\mid 2^r\). Consequently, for any natural number \(c\),
\[
(2^r+c)\bmod 2^k=c\bmod 2^k.
\]
In particular, if also \(c<2^k\), this residue is simply \(c\).

First consider
\[
m_1=2^{67}+1.
\]
Since \(1<2^{67}\), we have
\[
2^{67}\le m_1=2^{67}+1<2^{67}+2^{67}=2^{68}.
\]
Therefore \(\lfloor\log_2m_1\rfloor=67\), and the defining sum for \(F(m_1)\) has precisely the terms indexed by \(k=1,\ldots,67\). For every such \(k\), the power \(2^k\) divides \(2^{67}\), while \(1<2^k\). Hence
\[
m_1\bmod 2^k=(2^{67}+1)\bmod 2^k=1.
\]
There are 67 terms, so
\[
F(m_1)=\sum_{k=1}^{67}1=67.
\]
This is the familiar “trivial” occurrence of 67, at the index \(m_1=2^{67}+1\).

Now consider the different index
\[
m_2=2^{23}+3.
\]
We first determine the upper limit in the defining sum. Clearly \(2^{23}\le m_2\). Also \(3<2^{23}\), and therefore
\[
m_2=2^{23}+3<2^{23}+2^{23}=2^{24}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\lfloor\log_2m_2\rfloor=23.
\]
Thus
\[
F(m_2)=\sum_{k=1}^{23}\bigl((2^{23}+3)\bmod 2^k\bigr).
\]
There are two residue cases.

For \(k=1\), divisibility of \(2^{23}\) by 2 gives
\[
(2^{23}+3)\bmod 2=3\bmod 2=1.
\]

For every \(k\) with \(2\le k\le23\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{23}\), and \(3<2^k\) because \(2^k\ge4\). Hence
\[
(2^{23}+3)\bmod 2^k=3.
\]
There are \(23-1=22\) values of \(k\) in this second case. Therefore
\[
F(m_2)=1+22\cdot3=1+66=67.
\]
So \(67\) occurs in A049802 at the index \(m_2=2^{23}+3\) as well.

The two indices are distinct. Indeed,
\[
2^{23}+3<2^{24}\le2^{67}<2^{67}+1,
\]
where the first inequality follows again from \(3<2^{23}\). Thus \(m_2<m_1\).

We have consequently exhibited two distinct natural numbers \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) satisfying
\[
F(m_1)=F(m_2)=67.
\]
It follows directly from the definition of A383327 that
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts that \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\) in this set, so it would imply \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts the two distinct occurrences just constructed. Therefore the conjecture is false.
